title: Fifth Circuit Rejects the Server Test, Then Reinvents It
content: The court declines to adopt the server test’s fixation-based reasoning but reaches much the same result under a “transmit requirement” that adds a new permission question. I’ve seen a lot of obituaries for the server test this week. The Fifth Circuit certainly gave people material to work with. In Emmerich Newspapers, Inc. v. Particle Media, Inc. ( read the opinion here ), the court became the first federal appeals court to reject the Ninth Circuit’s nearly twenty-year-old test, concluding that its fixation-based reasoning rests on “weak statutory footing.” But read a few pages further and something very similar climbs back out of Crystal Lake wearing a different mask. The Fifth Circuit calls it a “transmit requirement.” Instead of asking where a copy of the work is stored , the court asks who actually transmits the content to the public. When an embed merely directs a browser to request the work from the copyright owner’s own server, the embedder isn’t the one transmitting it. That’s a different statutory theory, but the court acknowledged that the two approaches “end up in a similar place: a website cannot transmit a work that it does not have.” So, yes, the server test is dead in the Fifth Circuit. It just survived the part where it died. That doesn’t mean nothing’s changed. The new test also asks whether the transmission was permitted , bringing a copyright owner’s ability to block a transmission into the analysis for the first time. And shifting the focus from fixation to transmission may matter beyond embedded images. The server test’s fixation rationale is tied specifically to copyright’s display right; the Fifth Circuit’s transmission rationale should logically extend to the public performance right as well. title: UN committee warns of racial discrimination amid civilian deaths and mass displacement in Lebanon
content: The UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (CERD) on Wednesday called for an end to attacks directed against or indiscriminately affecting civilians in Lebanon. Acting under its Early Warning and Urgent Action Procedure , the Committee warned that no derogation from the prohibition of racial discrimination is permitted during armed conflict. Under the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination , which Israel ratified in 1979, states must prevent and eliminate racial discrimination, including ( as interpreted by CERD ) against non-citizens under a state’s “effective control.” Large‑scale displacement in a conflict zone can raise concerns under CERD when the effects fall disproportionately on a particular ethnic or national group, or when official statements dehumanize affected populations. CERD voiced concern over the civilian toll resulting from Israeli military operations in its war against Hezbollah. It again urged Israel to rescind “blanket displacement and evacuation orders” and to halt the forcible transfer of people across southern Lebanon. UN officials previously questioned whether these orders met the effectiveness requirements of international law. CERD reported that more than 360,000 people remained displaced at the end of July. The warnings, like this one posted on X earlier this month by the IDF’s Arabic-language spokesperson, call for immediate evacuation and warn that anyone who remains near military targets “exposes their life to danger.” CERD noted that more than 70 such orders were issued in March, affecting nearly 190 towns and villages. Hezbollah is an Shia Islamist paramilitary group based in Lebanon, which Israel labels as an Iranian-backed terrorist organization. title: UN raises concerns about rise in anti-migrant violence in South Africa
content: The UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (CERD) on Thursday expressed concern about the rise in violence and racist hate crimes targeting migrants in South Africa, urging authorities to implement urgent measures to address this issue. CERD reported a range of attacks perpetrated against migrants, including killings, displacement, abductions, looting, destruction of property, unlawful evictions, and restrictions on access to essential services, which all violate the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination . The committee also noted the proliferation of racist hate speech and the dissemination of negative stereotypes against migrants and refugees in South Africa, particularly by civic movements and through social media platforms. CERD further highlighted the inadequate response by law enforcement agencies to address the increasing xenophobia and violence against migrants, raising additional concerns about the persistence of racial profiling and racially motivated excessive use of force by law enforcement officials. Additionally, CERD criticized the absence of effective strategies to address the root causes of racial discrimination and violence against migrants, which include persistent socio-economic inequalities dating back to the apartheid era as well as delays in the issuance and renewal of migrants’ documents. Consequently, the committee called on authorities to implement measures to combat the formation of organised racist vigilante groups as well as proscribing and dismantling such organizations. It also recommended that authorities work with media outlets and Internet service providers to combat the spread of hate speech and harmful stereotypes online. It additionally urged the country’s authorities to ensure an objective and proportionate law-enforcement response to racist violence and to guarantee accountability through investigations of all reported abuses. title: Amnesty International urges Haiti to take accountability for lethal gang attacks in Kenscoff
content: Amnesty International on Wednesday condemned the deadly gang attack that occurred in Haiti’s Kenscoff commune earlier this week, leaving at least 47 dead, 22 injured, and dozens more apparently abducted. According to the human rights organization, many of those attacked were people seeking refuge in a church following violence. “Sadly, we are once again witnessing another massacre in Haiti. This is a reminder of the devastating human cost of the absence of effective policies to protect the population,” said Astrid Valencia, deputy regional director for research at Amnesty International. The UN also commented on the attacks, stating that armed men began setting homes on fire and attacking residents. By Monday morning, bodies had piled in the streets in the “once relatively peaceful area.” One gang leader reportedly threatened to kill the hostages if authorities killed any gang members. Haiti has been facing severe gang violence for years, particularly due to leaders’ weaponization of armed criminal groups to gain power and due to the lack of a strong centralized police force. Eventually, these criminal groups amassed greater power and influence than the politicians who initially relied on them. In addition to gang violence, sexual violence is exploited as a “weapon of terror” in the country and also serves to restrict access to humanitarian aid. According to a UN quarterly report , between April and June 2026 alone, over 1,400 people were killed, most by gangs, and at least 796 people were recorded as victims of gang-related sexual violence. The humanitarian crisis in Haiti is currently listed as one of the worst in the world. title: US district judge cancels nationwide ruling in lawsuit against Trump’s mail-in voting executive order
content: US District Judge Indira Talwani on Wednesday canceled her earlier ruling granting a preliminary injunction to prevent the US Postal Service (USPS) from implementing President Trump’s mail-in voting executive order (EO) on or before this year’s midterm elections. This latest development in the tumultuous legal battle over the EO directly follows a request by the US Department of Justice (DOJ) to reconsider her earlier ruling after the Supreme Court issued an adverse decision in a separate lawsuit against the order. The Supreme Court ruled Monday on a procedural issue in the suit Trump v. California , stating that the states bringing the challenge did not present an injury concrete or imminent enough to make their claim justiciable , meaning the Court could not hear the complaint. However, they have not yet ruled on any legal issues in the case. Trump’s controversial mail-in voting EO was issued in late March, with the indicated intention to enhance election integrity and security. The EO directs the US Department of Homeland Security to generate “state citizenship lists” using federal immigration and naturalization data so that only individuals on the list will be issued an absentee ballot. The order has been sharply criticized by organizations such as the Brennan Center for Justice, which point to the unreliability of the data and potential to block eligible citizens from voting. In Judge Talwani’s decision, she indicated that the Supreme Court believed her initial ruling came preliminarily, as the steps to carry out the effects of the EO had not yet been taken; USPS had not proposed or published their rule addressing their implementation methods at the time of the injunction. Despite the existence of Judge Talwani’s prior injunction barring them from doing so, USPS finalized its rule last week. It took effect on August 21. title: Two UN peacekeepers confirmed dead and several wounded after ambush in South Sudan
content: Two UN peacekeepers on Monday were killed in an ambush in South Sudan’s eastern Jonglei state, in an attack that the organization has stated may constitute a war crime under international law. The attack was the latest in a region shaken by renewed military conflict. The attack comes amid a re-inflammation of civil conflict in South Sudan dating back over 10 years . The UN Mission in South Sudan ( UNMISS ) operates in the nation under Chapter VII of the UN Charter, with the stated goal “ to prevent a return to civil war and an escalation of violence, facilitate the safe delivery of humanitarian assistance, monitor and report on human rights and the peace agreement.” Monday’s ambush struck a patrol traveling toward the remote area of Pajut, killing two Ethiopian peacekeepers and wounding seven others. UNMISS said that it deployed a Quick Reaction Force to secure the area and allow for emergency medical response. This marks the eighth and ninth peacekeepers to be killed in South Sudan this year. The head of UNMISS, Anita Kiki Gbeho, described the killings as “unacceptable” and called for “a thorough and prompt investigation to ensure that those responsible are brought to justice.” UN Officials have noted that Monday’s ambush may constitute a war crime . Under the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (ICC), war crimes include “Intentionally directing attacks against personnel, installations, material, units or vehicles involved in a humanitarian assistance or peacekeeping mission in accordance with the Charter of the United Nations…” Under Article 77 of the Rome Statute, international war crimes may carry a punishment of life imprisonment “when justified by the extreme gravity of the crime.” Last week, the UN Commission on Human Rights in South Sudan reported rising violence as the country is set to hold its first elections since its 2011 independence. title: A List of ICE Subpoenas to Tech Companies
content: Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has conducted unlawful investigations into dozens of individuals who have documented ICE activities in their communities, social media users who criticized the government, and international students who attended a protest. A favored tool in these speech chilling investigations are administrative subpoenas sent to technology companies, requesting basic subscriber data about their users. For example, from 2018 to 2020, ICE sent nearly 500 administrative subpoenas to Meta, Google, and Twitter (now X), according to documents obtained by Just Futures Law . In just the second half of 2025, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) sent 21 administrative subpoenas to Reddit, according to its Transparency Report . While some subpoenas are routine, ICE has been forced to withdraw others after users challenged them in court or companies pushed back . These challenged subpoenas exceeded the agency's statutory authority and violated users' First Amendment rights. Below is a non-comprehensive list of DHS subpoenas that we gathered going back to 2025, looking at public reporting and court cases. This is likely an undercount. The full scope is hard to pin down because these subpoenas typically only come to light when a user is given notice and challenges them in court, or when a company documents them in a transparency report (so far, only Reddit appears to break out specific numbers on DHS subpoenas). In addition, DHS has been slow to respond to our Freedom of Information Act requests and lawsuits seeking records that would show how many administrative subpoenas ICE has sent to social media companies since 2025. If you know of other subpoenas that are not on this list, please reach out to info@eff.org. While the government has abused the subpoena process in other areas , particularly to hospitals , this list focuses on DHS and ICE subpoenas to technology companies for user data. title: EFF's Policy Position on ALPR Surveillance: Eliminate It and Reduce Its Harms
content: Automated license plate readers (ALPRs) build a searchable map of everywhere a driver goes, fed into databases that police, ICE, and private vendors can query after the fact. Networked across a city, ALPRs are purpose-built to track everyone regardless of suspicion. ALPRs are not a surveillance tool that can be made safe with the right policy or feature update—they are irredeemably harmful. EFF's position is that ALPR mass surveillance—the indiscriminate, continuous collection and retention of location data on every driver, regardless of suspicion—should not exist. Because it nonetheless does, EFF also urges courts and state legislatures to impose strict, enforceable restrictions, such as warrant requirements and deletion deadlines.
